title: 'I believed I was dead,' RCMP officer tells inquest
subtitle: As he stared down the barrel of a rifle, Const. Peter Neily had a feeling he'd never experienced before and hasn't experienced since. "Right then, at that moment in time, I believed I was dead," Neily said. "There was that sudden realization that right then and there I was going to die."
article: As he stared down the barrel of a rifle, Const. Peter Neily had a feeling he'd never experienced before and hasn't experienced since.
"Right then, at that moment in time, I believed I was dead," Neily said. "There was that sudden realization that right then and there I was going to die."
Neily, an RCMP officer for almost nine years, told a jury at a coroner's inquest Monday about the moments leading up to the shooting that left 28-year-old Adam Brian Purdie dead on March 2, 2011.

Earlier that evening Purdie had fled a traffic stop on 16th Avenue in South Surrey when the officer who pulled him over spotted the butt of a rifle covered with a black jacket on the floor in front of the rear passenger seat. She called for backup and just before it arrived Purdie took off in his Chrysler 300.
She drove east on 16th after him, but was unable to locate Purdie's car.
He was spotted a short time later heading north on King George Boulevard near Highway 99. A senior officer ordered that there be no pursuit, and instead officers tried to intercept Purdie.
Neily was stopped on Highway 10 at King George facing west when Purdie approached. Another officer had just placed a spike belt on the road to try to disable the Chrysler.

From the driver's seat of his car, Neily saw Purdie's car go through the intersection, avoid the spike belt and collide with the two vehicles, one of which went off the road and crashed into a bus shelter.

Neily said Purdie then pulled over on the side of King George Highway. Because of previous radio transmissions, Neily knew that Purdie had a criminal record involving firearms, was subject to a firearms prohibition, was suicidal and had a history of violence and interactions with police.
"It was a life-threatening situation," Neily said.
Neily turned on to King George and decided to pin the Chrysler with his police car to immobilize it so that Purdie could be arrested.
"At that point I was fearful for the safety of the civilians in the area and also myself and the other officers, so I took the action that was required," Neily said.

Neily's car struck the Chrysler and came to a stop with his passenger-side window across from Purdie's driver's-side window. He said he looked over and saw Purdie's gun pointed in his direction and heard Purdie yell, "F--- you!"

Neily tried to stay out of sight - he said it wasn't possible to escape from his car safely - and pulled out his gun. He emptied 15 rounds into Purdie's car, but he could still see the barrel of the rifle.

"I couldn't believe that after all that gunfire we were still in the situation where this individual was still trying to shoot me," Neily said. "I thought, what's wrong with my bullets, why isn't it working?"

As Neily reloaded he heard Purdie shout profanities at him again and saw the rifle moving. Neily fired another 15 bullets at the Chrysler. When he couldn't see the gun any more, he got out of his police car and ran down the road to take cover behind another officer's vehicle.

Neily said he didn't recall saying anything to Purdie, however a bystander heard someone yell at Purdie multiple times to throw his gun out of the car and put his hands where he could see them. Neily was also unable to recall if Purdie fired his weapon.

Coroner's counsel asked Neily if at any point he saw Purdie withdraw the gun and point it under his own chin. A pathologist's report states that Purdie suffered 17 gunshot wounds, one of which was self-inflicted.
"I never saw that. What I did see was what the barrel of that gun looked like in my face," Neily said.
According to Purdie's autopsy, he died of multiple gunshot wounds. A toxicology report showed cocaine and morphine in Purdie's system.

At the end of the inquest, scheduled to wrap up Wednesday, the jury will render a written verdict - which will include classification of death - and make recommendations. The jury is supposed to determine facts, not assign blame.
An investigation conducted by the Saanich police cleared Neily of any wrongdoing.
